transcript: Submit Puzzle Ideas helps you make your own puzzle for NINETIMESNINE, step by step, and send it to the team. This video shows every entry, what it is for, and how it fits into the puzzle the wizard builds. On thelogicgrid.com, choose Submit Puzzle Ideas, under One account for every game. A box asks which puzzle you would like to make. Choose NINETIMESNINE. The wizard goes one step at a time. There are 5 steps, and you can jump back to any of them. Everything you type is saved on this device as you go. Leave and come back later, and your draft is waiting. Start over clears it when you want a fresh start.

Watch how it works opens this video and a written guide to every entry. Show help on every field shows what to write, an example, and how each entry is used in your puzzle. Step 1: Your story. Every NINETIMESNINE puzzle tells a short case: why the grid needs filling, and how it ends. Title, which is required. The name of your puzzle. Printed at the top of the puzzle and the PDF, and shown in Saved puzzles and in your credit.

Look. The look that suits your story best. Picks the pictures and colors when your puzzle is played in the game. Opening, which is required. One or two sentences: who needs the grid filled, and why. Shown above the grid and printed on the puzzle page, before the rules. What is at stake. One short sentence that makes it matter. Added after the opening, so players know why they are solving.

Ending, which is required. What happens when the grid is full. Shown when the puzzle is solved, and printed on the answer key. Step 2: The grid. Choose the size and rules of your grid, and who places the starting numbers. Grid size, which is required. 4 × 4 and 6 × 6 are quick; 9 × 9 is the classic size. Every row, column and box holds the numbers 1 to the size, each exactly once.

Diagonals too. Both long diagonals must also hold every number once. Adds an extra rule, which also means fewer starting numbers are needed. Who places the starting numbers?. Design the grid yourself, or let the wizard make one at the level you choose. Your numbers are checked: the puzzle must have exactly one answer, reachable by reasoning alone. Step 3: Starting numbers. Type the numbers players start with. Leave the other cells empty.

Starting numbers. Type a number in each cell that should start filled. Leave the rest empty. These are the numbers printed in the grid. The wizard checks there is exactly one way to fill the rest. Step 4: Pictures and sounds. Optional: add your own pictures and sounds for your puzzle. Pictures and sounds. Up to 3 pictures and 2 sounds that you made yourself. For each one, say what it is for, whether we may use it, and how to credit you. The team can use them with your puzzle in the game: a cover picture, a sound when it is solved, or background music.

At the bottom of every step, you see your storyline as you write it: the puzzle's words, just as players will read them. You cannot type in it. It changes as you fill in the fields above. Step 5: Credit and permission. How you would like to be credited, and your permission to use your puzzle. Author credit. The name shown in the author credits of your puzzle. Printed on your puzzle and shown in the game's credits if it is published.

Permission, which is required. Tick the box to say you made the puzzle yourself, and that the team may use and publish it with the credit you chose. We can only save and publish your puzzle with your permission. Check my puzzle opens a new page. The box at the top says whether your puzzle is ready: it must have exactly one answer that players can reason out. Anything missing or wrong is listed, with a link straight to the field, and suggestions to make it better. Every entry is here in one editor, so you can fix or change anything. Each change is checked again straight away, so you always know whether the puzzle is still valid.

When you are happy, press Build my puzzle. Download the PDF to keep or share it, or print it straight away. It has your puzzle and its answer key. Your puzzle is also saved to your Saved puzzles, so you can play it in the game, and a copy goes to the team, who may publish it with your credit. Want to change something? Make changes takes you back to the editor, with suggestions shown and the one-answer check, then build it again. Answer the questions, check and fix, then build, print and play. Have fun making puzzles!
